plan.chapterName: OpenStax Calculus, chapter 14: Differentiation of Functions of Several Variables
plan.contextChunk: This figure is a three-dimensional diagram pairing a shaded surface with a set of direction arrows and their projections onto the plane below. An upward-opening paraboloid, shaded cream at the left, blue across the right rim, and orange along its lower flank, is drawn with the z-axis rising through it, the y-axis running to the right, and the x-axis coming forward at the lower left. A black dot on the near face of the bowl is labeled P0 (x0, y0, z0) by a leader line to the right. Three kinds of arrows leave that dot: an orange one angling up and to the right along the steepest rise, a dark blue one angling down and to the left, and a pair of teal arrows lying along a teal curve that wraps horizontally around the bowl at constant height. Red and gray dashed drop lines carry the arrangement down to a small flat copy of itself on the plane, where the blue arrow is labeled minus grad f with the note Most rapid decrease in f, the orange arrow is labeled grad f with Most rapid increase in f, and the teal arrows are labeled Zero change in f, and a small square marks the right angle between the gradient direction and the level direction. Flattening the three directions into the plane is what makes that perpendicularity visible. The diagram illustrates how the directional derivative reaches its largest value along the gradient, its most negative value opposite the gradient, and zero along the level curve.

interactions.label: Direction angle at P0
interactions.teaches: The directional derivative is largest when the direction aligns with ∇f, zero when the direction is tangent to the level curve, and most negative when the direction points opposite ∇f

interactions.label: View
interactions.teaches: Flattening the arrows into the xy-plane makes the perpendicular relationship between the gradient and the level-curve direction visually explicit
Hovering a direction category identifies the matching surface and projected arrows, linking ∇f with maximum increase, -∇f with maximum decrease, and the teal tangent direction with zero change

demo_steps.title: Gradient direction: maximum increase
demo_steps.narration: At θ = 0°, the rotating direction arrow lines up with the orange gradient arrow. The directional derivative reaches its largest positive value because the motion is directly up the steepest slope.

demo_steps.title: Level direction: zero change
demo_steps.narration: At θ = 90°, the rotating arrow lies along the teal level curve. The height does not change to first order, so the directional derivative is zero.

demo_steps.title: Projected perpendicularity
demo_steps.narration: Switching to the plane projection flattens the same arrows below the surface. The right-angle marker shows that the gradient is perpendicular to the level direction.

demo_steps.title: Opposite gradient: maximum decrease
demo_steps.narration: At θ = 180°, the arrow points opposite the gradient, matching the dark blue direction. The directional derivative is most negative, indicating most rapid decrease in f.

interactionPlan.geometry_notes: Use world coordinates with +Z vertical, +Y visually to the right, and +X visually down-left, matching the source axes. Model the bowl as z = a(x^2 + y^2) with a = 0.22, radius r = 3.0, so the top rim is at z ≈ 1.98. Bowl center at the origin; axes span approximately x,y ∈ [-3.4, 3.7] and z ∈ [-1.6, 2.6]. Top rim should read as a broad ellipse in the axonometric view. Use P0 = (0.55, 1.65, 0.22(0.55^2 + 1.65^2)) ≈ (0.55, 1.65, 0.67), on the near-right flank of the bowl. The gradient in the xy-plane is ∇f = (2ax0, 2ay0) ≈ (0.24, 0.73), pointing mostly toward +Y/right and slightly toward +X/down-left. The orange surface arrow should start at P0, point outward/up along the tangent direction of ∇f, and have xy length about 0.75 with vertical rise |∇f| times that length. The dark blue arrow should start at P0 and point exactly opposite, with comparable length and downward visual slope. The teal level curve is the circle x^2 + y^2 = x0^2 + y0^2 at z = z0, drawn around the bowl at constant height; emphasize the front visible arc through P0. Teal tangent directions use unit vector perpendicular to ∇f in the xy-plane, approximately (-0.95, 0.32) and its opposite, with zero vertical change. The lower projection sits on a horizontal plane z = -1.25, directly below P0 and arrow endpoints. Projected orange, blue, and teal arrows share the same xy directions as the surface arrows but have z = -1.25. The right-angle marker is a small square of side about 0.12 world units at the projected point between the orange gradient direction and teal level direction. Color palette: gradient arrows orange-red #f05a28; negative-gradient arrows dark blue #1f4e79; level curve and zero-change arrows teal #159a9c; point P0 black #000000; axes black/dark gray #222222; dashed projection lines red #e84a5f and gray #777777; bowl interior cream #fff3d6 blending to pale blue #9fc7e8; exterior/lower flank orange #ff7f32 with light transparency or smooth shading. Directional derivative for the slider should be D_u f = |∇f| cos θ, where θ is measured from the gradient direction toward the teal level direction in the xy-plane. Display approximate values normalized by |∇f| if desired, e.g. D_u f / |∇f| = cos θ.
interactionPlan.notes: Render the paraboloid as a parametric mesh with vertex colors or a custom shader to reproduce the cream/blue/orange textbook shading; use double-sided material if necessary so the inner bowl and outer flank are both visible. Use TubeGeometry or thick line impostors for arrows so arrowheads remain readable in PDF embedding. For the view toggle, do not destroy geometry: fade the bowl and surface arrows down while enlarging/emphasizing the lower projection in Plane projection mode; in Surface arrows mode keep the lower projection visible but lighter, as in the source. The directionAngle slider should update both the surface rotating arrow and its lower projected copy, recoloring or annotating it according to sign: orange-positive near 0°, teal/neutral near 90° or 270°, blue-negative near 180°. Hover picking should include labels and arrows as one linked group per category so the corresponding surface arrow, projected arrow, and explanatory text highlight together.

- Slider for direction angle at P0: the learner rotates a direction arrow around the point, the projected arrow and directional derivative value update from maximum through zero to minimum, showing how alignment with the gradient controls the rate of change.

authoredContext:
Suppose the function z=f(x,y) is differentiable at (x0,y0) (the figure).

The ‖u‖ disappears because u is a unit vector. Therefore, the directional derivative is equal to the magnitude of the gradient evaluated at (x0,y0) multiplied by cosφ. Recall that cosφ ranges from −1 to 1. If φ=0, then cosφ=1 and ∇f(x0,y0) and u both point in the same direction. If φ=π, then cosφ=−1 and ∇f(x0,y0) and u point in opposite directions. In the first case, the value of Duf(x0,y0) is maximized; in the second case, the value of Duf(x0,y0) is minimized. If ∇f(x0,y0)=0, then Duf(x0,y0)=∇f(x0,y0)·u=0 for any vector u. These three cases are outlined in the following theorem.

The gradient indicates the maximum and minimum values of the directional derivative at a point.

An upward facing paraboloid in xyz space with point P0 (x0, y0, z0). From this point, there are arrows going up, down, and around the paraboloid. On the xy plane, the point (x0, y0) is marked, and the corresponding arrows are drawn onto the plane: the down arrow corresponds to −∇f (most rapid decrease in f), the up arrow corresponds to ∇f (most rapid increase in f), and the arrows around correspond to no change in f. The up/down arrows are perpendicular to the around arrows in their projection on the plane.

The figure shows a portion of the graph of the function f(x,y)=3+sinxsiny. Given a point (a,b) in the domain of f, the maximum value of the gradient at that point is given by ‖∇f(a,b)‖. This would equal the rate of greatest ascent if the surface represented a topographical map. If we went in the opposite direction, it would be the rate of greatest descent.

discrepancies: Initial viewpoint is rotated/mirrored relative to the source: the x axis points to the right and y to the lower-left, while the source has x lower-left and y right, changing the apparent placement of P0 and the projection diagram.
The orange highlighted surface region does not match the source's broad front/underside shading; it appears as a side stripe/sector on the left rather than a continuous orange front face of the bowl.

P0 and its surface arrows are visually crowded and partly obscured near the bowl edge, whereas the source clearly places P0 on the right side of the surface with separated gradient, negative-gradient, and tangent arrows.
The lower projected arrow diagram is too compressed relative to the source and sits very close to the surface labels, reducing the clear separation between the 3D surface and xy-plane projection.
Several labels are misplaced or crowded around the surface point, especially the P0 label and 'Most rapid decrease in f', compared with the clean leader-line layout in the source.
evaluation.notes: The generated figure captures the main gradient, level-curve, and projection concept well with useful interactions, but the initial orientation, orange surface shading, and crowded label placement reduce fidelity to the textbook figure.
action_items: Adjust the initial camera/view so the axes match the source orientation: z vertical, x down-left, and y to the right.
Rework the orange surface shading to cover the front/underside portion of the paraboloid rather than appearing as a left-side sector stripe.
Move P0 farther to the right side of the visible surface and separate the surface arrows and P0 label so they match the source's clearer layout.
Increase spacing between the surface diagram and the lower projected xy-plane arrows to better match the source composition.

feedback.rationale: The concept and interactivity are strong, but the remaining issues are concrete rendering/layout fixes—camera orientation, shading placement, spacing, and label crowding—best handled by the generator.

demo_steps.title: Gradient direction: maximum increase
demo_steps.narration: At θ = 0°, the rotating direction arrow lines up with the orange gradient arrow. The directional derivative reaches its largest positive value because the motion is directly up the steepest slope.

demo_steps.title: Level direction: zero change
demo_steps.narration: At θ = 90°, the rotating arrow lies along the teal level curve. The height does not change to first order, so the directional derivative is zero.

demo_steps.title: Projected perpendicularity
demo_steps.narration: Switching to the plane projection flattens the same arrows below the surface. The right-angle marker shows that the gradient is perpendicular to the level direction.

demo_steps.title: Opposite gradient: maximum decrease
demo_steps.narration: At θ = 180°, the arrow points opposite the gradient, matching the dark blue direction. The directional derivative is most negative, indicating most rapid decrease in f.

interactionPlan.geometry_notes: Use world coordinates with +Z vertical, +Y visually to the right, and +X visually down-left, matching the source axes. Model the bowl as z = a(x^2 + y^2) with a = 0.22, radius r = 3.0, so the top rim is at z ≈ 1.98. Bowl center at the origin; axes span approximately x,y ∈ [-3.4, 3.7] and z ∈ [-1.6, 2.6]. Top rim should read as a broad ellipse in the axonometric view. Use P0 = (0.55, 1.65, 0.22(0.55^2 + 1.65^2)) ≈ (0.55, 1.65, 0.67), on the near-right flank of the bowl. The gradient in the xy-plane is ∇f = (2ax0, 2ay0) ≈ (0.24, 0.73), pointing mostly toward +Y/right and slightly toward +X/down-left. The orange surface arrow should start at P0, point outward/up along the tangent direction of ∇f, and have xy length about 0.75 with vertical rise |∇f| times that length. The dark blue arrow should start at P0 and point exactly opposite, with comparable length and downward visual slope. The teal level curve is the circle x^2 + y^2 = x0^2 + y0^2 at z = z0, drawn around the bowl at constant height; emphasize the front visible arc through P0. Teal tangent directions use unit vector perpendicular to ∇f in the xy-plane, approximately (-0.95, 0.32) and its opposite, with zero vertical change. The lower projection sits on a horizontal plane z = -1.25, directly below P0 and arrow endpoints. Projected orange, blue, and teal arrows share the same xy directions as the surface arrows but have z = -1.25. The right-angle marker is a small square of side about 0.12 world units at the projected point between the orange gradient direction and teal level direction. Color palette: gradient arrows orange-red #f05a28; negative-gradient arrows dark blue #1f4e79; level curve and zero-change arrows teal #159a9c; point P0 black #000000; axes black/dark gray #222222; dashed projection lines red #e84a5f and gray #777777; bowl interior cream #fff3d6 blending to pale blue #9fc7e8; exterior/lower flank orange #ff7f32 with light transparency or smooth shading. Directional derivative for the slider should be D_u f = |∇f| cos θ, where θ is measured from the gradient direction toward the teal level direction in the xy-plane. Display approximate values normalized by |∇f| if desired, e.g. D_u f / |∇f| = cos θ.
interactionPlan.notes: Render the paraboloid as a parametric mesh with vertex colors or a custom shader to reproduce the cream/blue/orange textbook shading; use double-sided material if necessary so the inner bowl and outer flank are both visible. Use TubeGeometry or thick line impostors for arrows so arrowheads remain readable in PDF embedding. For the view toggle, do not destroy geometry: fade the bowl and surface arrows down while enlarging/emphasizing the lower projection in Plane projection mode; in Surface arrows mode keep the lower projection visible but lighter, as in the source. The directionAngle slider should update both the surface rotating arrow and its lower projected copy, recoloring or annotating it according to sign: orange-positive near 0°, teal/neutral near 90° or 270°, blue-negative near 180°. Hover picking should include labels and arrows as one linked group per category so the corresponding surface arrow, projected arrow, and explanatory text highlight together.

plan.authoredPrompt: This figure is a three-dimensional diagram pairing a shaded surface with a set of direction arrows and their projections onto the plane below. An upward-opening paraboloid, shaded cream at the left, blue across the right rim, and orange along its lower flank, is drawn with the z-axis rising through it, the y-axis running to the right, and the x-axis coming forward at the lower left. A black dot on the near face of the bowl is labeled P0 (x0, y0, z0) by a leader line to the right. Three kinds of arrows leave that dot: an orange one angling up and to the right along the steepest rise, a dark blue one angling down and to the left, and a pair of teal arrows lying along a teal curve that wraps horizontally around the bowl at constant height. Red and gray dashed drop lines carry the arrangement down to a small flat copy of itself on the plane, where the blue arrow is labeled minus grad f with the note Most rapid decrease in f, the orange arrow is labeled grad f with Most rapid increase in f, and the teal arrows are labeled Zero change in f, and a small square marks the right angle between the gradient direction and the level direction. Flattening the three directions into the plane is what makes that perpendicularity visible. The diagram illustrates how the directional derivative reaches its largest value along the gradient, its most negative value opposite the gradient, and zero along the level curve.
plan.authoredInteractions:
- Slider for direction angle at P0: the learner rotates a direction arrow around the point, the projected arrow and directional derivative value update from maximum through zero to minimum, showing how alignment with the gradient controls the rate of change.
- Toggle between surface arrows and plane projection: the learner switches views, the 3D arrows flatten to the diagram below with the right-angle marker on the level direction, making the perpendicular relationship between gradient and level curve easier to see.
- Hover for direction categories: the learner hovers grad f, -grad f, or the teal level direction, the matching surface arrow and label highlight, clarifying maximum increase, maximum decrease, and zero change at P0.
